scenes.text: Close your eyes and walk into your family's living room in nineteen sixty-five. Your feet sink into the carpet. The television is warming up in the corner. Something is ticking on the wall. There's a smell of furniture polish, coffee and maybe a little cigarette smoke. And everything is exactly where it has always been.
scenes.caption: WALK INTO 1965

scenes.text: The living room of the sixties was the heart of the American home. It was where the family watched television, where company was received, where Christmas happened, and where children were told, more than once, not to put their feet on the furniture.
scenes.caption: THE HEART OF THE HOME

scenes.text: So today, let's count down twenty-five things that almost every nineteen sixties living room had. Count how many your family had. I'll bet it's more than twenty.
scenes.caption: COUNT THEM

scenes.text: And one quick note. In many homes, there were really two living rooms. The everyday room where the family watched television, and the good room, or the front parlor, that was kept perfect for guests, holidays and the minister's visit. Children were hardly allowed to set foot in the good room. You'll see a little of both on our list.
scenes.caption: THE GOOD ROOM

scenes.text: Number twenty-five. The plastic slipcovers. In many homes, the good couch was covered in clear, heavy plastic to keep it new. It squeaked when you sat down. In summer, it stuck to the backs of your legs. And when company came, the covers might come off, just for the evening, then go right back on.
scenes.caption: 25. PLASTIC SLIPCOVERS

scenes.text: Number twenty-four. The candy dish. A glass or cut-crystal dish on the coffee table, full of ribbon candy, butterscotch disks, or those strawberry candies wrapped to look like strawberries. At grandma's house, the candies in the dish had sometimes fused together into one solid lump that nobody dared to touch.
scenes.caption: 24. THE CANDY DISH

scenes.text: Number twenty-three. The big glass ashtray. In the sixties, roughly four in ten adults smoked, and every living room had ashtrays, even in homes where nobody smoked, for the guests. Heavy glass, amber or green, sometimes as big as a dinner plate. And a table lighter shaped like a little statue or a chess piece.
scenes.caption: 23. THE ASHTRAY

scenes.text: Number twenty-two. The console television. Not a small set, but a piece of furniture. A long wooden cabinet, sometimes with sliding doors, with a screen in the middle. Through most of the sixties, many families still watched in black and white, with three or four channels. Color sets were expensive, and they took over slowly.
scenes.caption: 22. THE CONSOLE TV

scenes.text: Turning on that television was a little ceremony. You pulled the knob, and a tiny dot of light appeared in the middle of the screen. Then you waited, maybe half a minute, while the tubes warmed up. Late at night, the station signed off with the national anthem, and then a test pattern with an Indian head drawing, and a long, high tone.
scenes.caption: THE TEST PATTERN

scenes.text: Number twenty-one. The rabbit ears. On top of the television sat an antenna with two long metal rods. When the picture got snowy, someone had to get up and move them. Sometimes the best picture came only when a child stood holding them. Some families added a piece of aluminum foil to the tips, just in case it helped.
scenes.caption: 21. THE RABBIT EARS

scenes.text: Number twenty. The hi-fi stereo console. Another long wooden cabinet, this one with a record player hidden under a lid, a radio, and speakers behind cloth. It played Frank Sinatra, Herb Alpert, the soundtrack to The Sound of Music and Christmas albums from the gas station. Children were warned never to touch the needle.
scenes.caption: 20. THE HI-FI

scenes.text: Number nineteen. Wall-to-wall carpet. By the sixties, the hardwood floors of earlier decades were covered over. Shag carpet came later in the decade, but even before that, families loved thick carpet in gold, avocado green, burnt orange or beige. Some people vacuumed it in a crosshatch pattern so it looked perfect.
scenes.caption: 19. WALL-TO-WALL CARPET

scenes.text: Number eighteen. The recliner. Dad's chair. It might have been a La-Z-Boy, the brand that made the reclining chair famous. Nobody else sat in it when he was home. Children who did were quickly told to move. And on Sunday afternoons, it became a place for a nap with the football game on.
scenes.caption: 18. DAD'S CHAIR

scenes.text: On the arms and the back of that chair, and on the couch too, there were doilies. Little lace or crocheted covers, often made by a grandmother, to protect the fabric from hair oil and dirty hands. Men's hair tonic of the time was so greasy that furniture makers sold covers for exactly that reason. They called them antimacassars.
scenes.caption: THE DOILIES

scenes.text: Number seventeen. The TV tray. Folding metal tables with painted flowers or patterns, stored in a little rack in the corner. On special nights, the family ate TV dinners off them while watching Bonanza or The Wonderful World of Disney. Swanson TV dinners came in aluminum trays, with turkey, peas, potatoes and a little dessert.
scenes.caption: 17. THE TV TRAY

scenes.text: Number sixteen. The TV Guide. It sat on top of the television, or on the coffee table, with that week's listings. It was the most-read magazine in America in the sixties, with millions of copies every week. Kids circled the shows they wanted to see, and the fall preview issue was a big event every September.
scenes.caption: 16. THE TV GUIDE

scenes.text: Number fifteen. The sunburst clock. A clock on the wall with metal rays shooting out in every direction, like a starburst. It was the height of modern style. Some had a little electric hum. Many families also had a wall clock that chimed every hour, which visitors loved and children learned to sleep through.
scenes.caption: 15. THE SUNBURST CLOCK

scenes.text: Number fourteen. The telephone table. Or, in many houses, the telephone was in the hallway, on a little table with a seat and a shelf for the phone book. The phone was black or beige, with a rotary dial. Later in the decade, there might be a colorful Princess phone. And there was one phone for the whole family.
scenes.caption: 14. THE TELEPHONE TABLE

scenes.text: Number thirteen. The encyclopedias. A full set of World Book or Britannica, lined up on a shelf, sometimes bought one volume at a time from the grocery store, or from a salesman who came to the door. Children used them for school reports, and parents were proud of them. Many sets ended at the letter S because the family stopped buying.
scenes.caption: 13. THE ENCYCLOPEDIAS

scenes.text: Next to them, there might be a row of Reader's Digest Condensed Books, in matching covers, arriving in the mail four times a year. A family photo album with black paper pages and little corner tabs. And a big dictionary on a stand. For many families, that shelf was their home library, and it was read over and over again.
scenes.caption: THE HOME LIBRARY

scenes.text: Number twelve. The family Bible. A big, heavy book with a soft leather cover, often on a table of its own. Inside the front cover were records of family births, marriages and deaths, written in different hands over the years. In many families, that Bible is still the most important record they have.
scenes.caption: 12. THE FAMILY BIBLE

scenes.text: Number eleven. The picture window. Many new houses of the fifties and sixties had a big picture window facing the street. It let in light, and showed off the living room to the neighbors. And in front of it, families often placed a lamp, a plant or a statue, so it looked nice from the outside.
scenes.caption: 11. THE PICTURE WINDOW

scenes.text: Number ten. The swag lamp. A hanging lamp on a chain, looped across the ceiling and plugged into the wall. Some had glass globes in amber or red. Others had a lamp on the end table with a pleated shade still wrapped in its plastic cover, years after it was bought.
scenes.caption: 10. THE SWAG LAMP

scenes.text: Number nine. The family portraits. On the wall, or on top of the television, there were framed pictures. Wedding photos. School pictures of every child, updated every year, with the same awkward smile. A photo of a son in uniform. And the formal family portrait from the department store studio, with everyone in matching outfits.
scenes.caption: 9. THE SCHOOL PICTURES

scenes.text: Number eight. The houseplants. A spider plant hanging in a macrame holder. A rubber tree in the corner. African violets on the windowsill. And sometimes plastic flowers, which were very fashionable and never needed watering. The dust collected on them, but that was a small price to pay.
scenes.caption: 8. THE PLANTS

scenes.text: Number seven. The coffee table. Long and low, made of wood, sometimes with a glass top. On it sat the candy dish, the ashtray, a few magazines like Life, Look, Reader's Digest and The Saturday Evening Post, and maybe a big coffee table book about the national parks.
scenes.caption: 7. THE COFFEE TABLE

scenes.text: Number six. The knick-knack shelf. A small wall shelf or a glass cabinet, filled with little figurines. Hummel children, porcelain birds, salt and pepper shakers from vacation, a tiny Eiffel Tower, souvenir spoons and a ceramic dog. Everything was dusted every week, and children were not allowed to play anywhere near it.
scenes.caption: 6. THE KNICK-KNACKS

scenes.text: Number five. The piano or organ. Many families had an upright piano, often handed down from grandparents, and children took weekly lessons. In the sixties, home organs from companies like Hammond and Lowrey became popular too. Every Christmas, someone played carols while the whole family sang.
scenes.caption: 5. THE PIANO

scenes.text: And next to the piano, often, a sewing basket. Mothers and grandmothers knitted and crocheted in the living room every evening, while the television played. Afghan blankets in orange, brown and yellow squares were draped over the back of the couch. Almost every family had at least one, and many still do today.
scenes.caption: THE AFGHAN BLANKET

scenes.text: Number four. The bowling trophies and the souvenirs. On a shelf, or on top of the television, there were trophies from the bowling league, the Little League or the church softball team. And next to them, souvenirs from the family vacation. A plate from Niagara Falls, a pennant from the Grand Canyon, and a little bear from Yellowstone.
scenes.caption: 4. THE TROPHIES

scenes.text: Number three. The bar cart or the liquor cabinet. Many living rooms of the sixties had a little bar, with highball glasses, an ice bucket, a cocktail shaker and bottles of whiskey and gin. When friends came over on a Saturday night, Dad mixed martinis and Mom put out bowls of mixed nuts and cheese balls.
scenes.caption: 3. THE BAR CART

scenes.text: Number two. The Christmas tree spot. Every living room had one corner that, once a year, became the most magical place in the house. In the sixties, it might hold a real tree, or a brand-new aluminum tree that glittered under a rotating color wheel. Bubble lights, tinsel and big colored bulbs filled the room with light.
scenes.caption: 2. THE CHRISTMAS CORNER

scenes.text: And number one. The family itself, all together, in one room. Before every child had a screen of their own, the living room was where everyone ended up at the end of the day. Dad in his recliner, Mom on the couch with her knitting, and the kids on the floor in front of the television, close enough to get a lecture about ruining their eyes.
scenes.caption: 1. THE FAMILY

scenes.text: So why do we remember those living rooms so clearly? Because nothing ever moved. The same couch, the same lamp, the same clock for twenty years. Families didn't redecorate every few years. Furniture was bought to last, and it did.
scenes.caption: NOTHING EVER MOVED

scenes.text: And because those rooms held our childhoods. The Christmas mornings, the Sunday nights watching Ed Sullivan, the moon landing in nineteen sixty-nine, when the whole family sat on the floor and watched in silence. We didn't know it then, but every evening there was a memory in the making.
scenes.caption: A MEMORY IN THE MAKING

scenes.text: So tell us in the comments. How many of these twenty-five did your family have? And what's one thing in your living room I didn't mention? We read every comment. Next time, we're going back to growing up in nineteen seventy-two, the forgotten decade. Thank you for spending this time with me.
scenes.caption: HOW MANY DID YOU HAVE?
